notes: Copyright reversionary interest under 1956 Act transitional provisions; statutory construction and 1973 assignment interpretation are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Assignability of reversionary copyright interest under 1956 Act
key_facts: Composer Richard Addinsell assigned film-score copyrights to Keith Prowse in the 1940s and executed a further 1973 assignment to the defendant.
All disputed works were created before 1 June 1957 and the reversionary interest in the last 25 years of copyright was in issue.
The claimant relied on a 2000 assignment from Addinsell's trustees; the defendant relied on the 1973 assignment.
The sole issue was whether a living author could assign the reversionary interest after commencement of the 1956 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial on ownership of reversionary copyright in pre-1957 musical works.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; declaration that the 1973 assignment effectively transferred the reversionary interest to the defendant.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 7 paragraph 28(3) of the Copyright Act 1956 did not apply the 1911 Act proviso to post-commencement assignments of existing works, so section 36 permitted a living author after 1 June 1957 to assign the reversionary interest; on its true construction the 1973 assignment conveyed the whole copyright including that interest.
legal_issues: Whether transitional provisions preserved the 1911 Act bar on assigning reversionary copyright after 1957
Construction of paragraph 28(3) of Schedule 7 to the 1956 Act
Whether the 1973 assignment included the reversionary interest
linked_authorities: Redwood Music Ltd v Francis, Day & Hunter [1978] RPC 429
Gregory Committee Report (Cmnd 8662)

notes: Long secure-tenancy disrepair appeal; damages methodology and costs/set-off rulings are detailed though procedural history is complex.

enrichment.short_title: Damages for secure tenancy disrepair and failure to mitigate
key_facts: Mr Shine, a secure tenant in a disrepair flat in Bethnal Green, sued English Churches Housing Group for section 11 breaches over about seven years.
The landlord accepted liability; the county court awarded £19,000 damages but the tenant unreasonably refused to vacate for repairs.
Proceedings were protracted with numerous interlocutory orders, injunctions and a High Court appeal by the tenant.
The landlord appealed the quantum, reserved costs orders and refusal to set off £1,500 costs awarded on an interlocutory appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Landlord's appeal from Shoreditch County Court award of disrepair damages to a secure tenant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; damages reduced from £19,000 to £8,000; landlord permitted to set off £1,500 costs and awarded costs of specified interlocutory hearings.
enrichment.ratio: Damages for breach of an implied section 11 repairing covenant should reflect the tenant's failure to mitigate, including unreasonable refusal to vacate for works and breach of court orders; a substantial discount is appropriate for the post-proceedings period; costs ordered on interlocutory applications may be set off against damages.
legal_issues: Method of assessing disrepair damages for secure tenants
Effect of failure to mitigate and refusal of alternative accommodation
Whether reserved interlocutory costs should be determined post-judgment
Set-off of costs awarded on an interlocutory appeal against damages

notes: Complex Kosovo shooting liability judgment; self-defence, combat immunity and transferred malice analysis are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Kosovo peacekeeping shooting: negligence and trespass liability
key_facts: British soldiers in the KFOR peacekeeping force shot at a car in Pristina on 2 July 1999 during independence celebrations.
Two passengers were killed and claimants Mohamet and Skender Bici were injured; Fahri Bici on the car roof had an AK47.
Soldiers claimed self-defence; forensic evidence indicated he was shot from behind and was not aiming at them.
Liability was tried under English law; the Ministry of Defence accepted vicarious liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Split trial on liability in negligence and trespass arising from Kosovo shooting.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded in negligence; Mohamet Bici also succeeded in battery by transferred malice; damages to be assessed; combat immunity and lack of duty of care rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Self-defence in civil claims requires an honest and reasonable belief of imminent attack, which was not established; combat immunity does not apply to peacekeeping policing where soldiers were not in active combat; transferred malice permits a non-targeted injured passenger to sue in battery; soldiers owed ordinary duties of care during peacekeeping operations.
legal_issues: Whether soldiers acted in reasonable self-defence
Applicability of combat immunity to UN peacekeeping
Whether a duty of care was owed to Kosovar claimants
Transferred malice in battery and assault claims
Wilkinson v Downton and psychiatric injury
Contributory negligence

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful deportation during pending asylum appeal
key_facts: Cameroonian claimant R(T) claimed asylum separately from his brothers, whose human rights appeals had succeeded.
His asylum appeal was dismissed and he was removed to Cameroon on 8 July 2003 despite an out-of-time tribunal application faxed that day.
Removal was conceded unlawful; the tribunal had refused permission to appeal on the basis the appeal was abandoned.
The Secretary of State undertook to secure return if permission to appeal succeeded but resisted immediate injunctive relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of removal decision and Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded; tribunal decision quashed and remitted; Secretary of State undertook to take steps to return claimant; costs to claimant; permission to appeal granted on section 104 construction.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Secretary of State has acted unlawfully by removing a claimant during a pending appeal, exposing him to risk of human rights violations, injunctive relief requiring steps to secure return is appropriate where the claimant cannot effectively instruct solicitors from abroad; discretionary relief must account for unlawful executive conduct.
legal_issues: Whether injunctive relief should require immediate return pending tribunal reconsideration
Effect of unlawful removal on pending asylum/human rights appeals
Construction of section 104 of the 2002 Act

notes: Products liability policy construction on assumed facts; Court of Appeal endorsed caution on hypothetical declarations.

enrichment.short_title: Products liability cover for cinema complex closure losses
key_facts: Ceiling collapse in one auditorium of a Manchester cinema complex built by Horbury led AMC to close all 16 auditoria pending inspection.
Wrong washers in suspended ceilings were assumed to have caused the collapse and latent defects in other auditoria.
Horbury sought declarations on its products liability policy before any third-party claim was issued.
The insurer denied cover for loss of profits from closure of unaffected auditoria.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court declarations on construction of an all-risks/products liability policy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; loss of profits from closure of the wider complex not covered by the policy.
enrichment.ratio: Under a products liability policy indemnifying liability in respect of loss of or damage to property caused by products, the phrase 'in respect of' limits cover to physical consequences of the occurrence; voluntary closure to inspect other auditoria after one ceiling collapse is not such a consequence and differs from losses flowing directly from physical damage in the affected auditorium.
legal_issues: Construction of 'in respect of loss of or damage to Property' in clause 4.1
Whether loss of profits from whole-complex closure is covered
Appropriateness of declarations on assumed facts before third-party liability established
Application of Rodan and Screenprint authorities

enrichment.short_title: Human rights challenge to agricultural notice-to-remedy procedure
key_facts: Lancashire County Council sought possession of Pollards Farm from tenant Mr Taylor after non-work Form 3 notices to remedy breaches.
The tenant processed milk and fruit juices on the holding in breach of agricultural-use covenants from 1990.
Arbitration and Court of Appeal proceedings had upheld a valid notice to quit before the Human Rights Act challenge.
The tenant argued Form 3 notices lacked the arbitration protections available for repair notices and breached Articles 6, 8 and A1P1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Possession claim with counterclaim seeking declaration of incompatibility; Secretary of State intervened.
enrichment.outcome: County Council entitled to possession; human rights and incompatibility claims dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Tenants served with non-work notices to remedy retain access to the ordinary courts before any notice to quit; differences between Form 2 and Form 3 procedures concern substantive security of tenure rather than Article 6 procedure and are justified where Parliament addressed a specific mischief of abusive repair notices; Article 8 and A1P1 do not prevent enforcement of a lawfully terminated agricultural tenancy.

enrichment.short_title: Negligence of trial counsel over omitted alibi direction
key_facts: Chetan Popat was wrongly convicted of attempted rape in 1997 and imprisoned before acquittal on retrial in 1999.
He sued defence counsel Miss Barnes for failing to request an alibi direction and not raising its absence on first appeal.
Counsel and client agreed not to invite the direction at trial because it might suggest his parents lied.
The Court of Appeal on the second appeal quashed convictions partly for absence of an alibi direction among other summing-up defects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for solicitor/barrister negligence causing loss of chance at trial and first appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; counsel not negligent at trial or on appeal 1.
enrichment.ratio: A competent criminal advocate could reasonably decide not to invite an alibi direction where the prosecution had not attacked the alibi as fabricated and a direction risked focusing the jury on possible lies by the defendant's parents; a tactical trial decision not to seek a direction is a strong reason not to raise its omission as a ground of appeal unless counsel's judgment was untenable.
legal_issues: Whether failure to invite alibi direction at trial was negligent
Whether omission should have been raised on first appeal
Status of alibi/Lucas directions in 1997-98 practice
Loss of chance assessment for wrongful conviction
Causation where tactical decision underlay omission

enrichment.short_title: Bank guarantee enforcement after Televillage receivership
key_facts: Triodos Bank lent to Acorn Televillages Ltd for a Crickhowell development secured by debenture and Mr Dobbs' personal guarantee.
Joint administrative receivers sold the Welsh site for £2.1m but not Acorn USA shares.
Mr Dobbs and Acorn brought extensive claims against the bank and receivers alleging breach of duty and conspiracy.
The bank sought judgment on the guarantee for about £50,000 outstanding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of guarantee claim with cross-claims against bank and receivers.

enrichment.ratio: Unless damages for the bank's failure to exercise step-in rights between October and December 2002 would exceed the guarantee shortfall (minus £50,000), Acorn's cross-claim gives the guarantor no defence; on the evidence receivers acted professionally and the bank's conduct did not breach duties owed.

notes: Planning appeal on gypsy status after Wrexham; inspector's voluntary-ill-health distinction held erroneous.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy status lost on permanent cessation of travelling

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Basildon District Council appealed against an inspector's grant of personal planning permission for up to four mobile homes and four touring caravans.
Mrs Doran and her extended family claimed Romany gypsy status but had decided to settle permanently at the site.
The inspector treated cessation of travelling due to ill health as involuntary and therefore compatible with retaining gypsy status.
The Secretary of State conceded the decision could not be supported following Wrexham.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288/289 appeal against planning inspector's enforcement appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; planning permissions quashed and decision remitted for redetermination; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Gypsy status under planning law is a functional test of nomadic habit of life at the time of determination; permanently retiring from travelling for ill health, age or choice ends that status regardless of voluntariness, though temporary inability to travel may not; Circular 1/94 supports nomadic lifestyle accommodation not permanent retirement sites.
legal_issues: Whether ill-health-driven permanent settlement preserves gypsy status
Correct application of Hearne and Wrexham authorities
Construction of personal planning permission conditions
Distinction between temporary and permanent cessation of travelling

enrichment.short_title: Right of way linked to modified restrictive covenant use
key_facts: 1965 conveyance granted NFU Trust a right of way over Manor House Drive for uses authorised by a restrictive covenant limiting the Manor House to offices.
Mr and Mrs McDonald owned the Manor House and applied under section 84 to modify the covenant for holiday lettings and a fitness centre.
Mr Hotchkin contended the right of way remained frozen at the 1965 authorised uses regardless of any Lands Tribunal modification.
Lands Tribunal proceedings were stayed pending construction of the easement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from declaration on construction of express grant of right of way.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; right of way may be used for purposes permitted following any section 84 discharge or modification of the user covenant.
enrichment.ratio: Where a 1965 grant links a right of way to lawful use of the dominant tenement 'authorised' by an adjoining restrictive covenant, section 84's possibility of non-consensual modification was a circumstance existing at grant; if the user covenant is modified or discharged the right of way extends to the modified lawful uses, otherwise the dominant owner could be left with lawful use but no access.
legal_issues: Whether easement use is fixed at date of grant or follows modified covenant
Interaction of section 84 modification with express easement grants
Construction of 'authorised by clause D in the Schedule'
Whether Lands Tribunal can vary easements
